traveler: Ibn Arabi (Muhyi al-Din Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn al-Arabi al-Ha'timi al-Ta'i)
title: Murcia to Damascus: the Seal of the Muhammadan Saints
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Murcia and the Making of a Seer

stops.name: Murcia, birth in the house of Ali ibn Muhammad
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of Ramadan in the year 560, a son is born in Murcia to Ali ibn Muhammad, a captain in the service of the emir Ibn Mardanish, and to his wife. They name him Muhammad, and he will be called Muhyi al-Din, the Reviver of the Religion, and in time simply al-Shaykh al-Akbar, the Greatest Master. His lineage runs to the Arab tribe of Ta'i, to Hatim al-Ta'i, proverbial for generosity. The kingdom of Murcia is a small independent taifa still holding out against the Almohads; the boy's first years pass under its own banner.
suggested_refs: The Taifa of Murcia under Ibn Mardanish, independent of the Almohad Caliphate until 1172
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur: The Life of Ibn 'Arabi
Stephen Hirtenstein, The Unlimited Mercifier
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the West (1165-1200)' (anqa.co.uk)

stops.name: Seville, the family removes from fallen Murcia
stops.campa: Murcia falls to the Almohad Caliphate and Ibn Mardanish's line ends; Ali ibn Muhammad takes his household west to Seville, capital of Almohad al-Andalus, where the boy of eight will spend the next twenty-seven years. Seville is a city of canals, orange trees, and the great minaret rising over the mosque; here he receives the ordinary schooling of a well-born youth, memorizing Qur'an and grammar, drawn for a time to the diversions natural to his age before the pull toward the inward life begins to show itself.
suggested_refs: The Giralda minaret of the Almohad Great Mosque of Seville, standing in his boyhood city
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the West (1165-1200)'

stops.name: Seville, the calling and the vision of the three prophets
stops.campa: In the middle of a night's party in Seville a voice calls to him out of nowhere: O Muhammad, it was not for this that you were created. He flees the company and shuts himself for days in a cemetery among the graves. There the vision comes: three figures standing together, Jesus, Moses, and Muhammad, each with an instruction for him — asceticism, the sciences of unveiling, and the seal who confirms both. He wakes changed, the amusements of his youth finished in an hour. His father, sensing the gravity of it, resolves to bring him before the one man in Cordoba who can weigh such a thing on the scale of philosophy: Ibn Rushd, called in the West Averroes.
stops.quote: O Muhammad, it was not for this that you were created.
stops.quote_source: The voice heard at Seville, in Ibn Arabi's account of his conversion; traditional biography after al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya
suggested_refs: Ibn Arabi's own account of his conversion in al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, Chapter 20
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
William Chittick, The Sufi Path of Knowledge
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the West (1165-1200)'

stops.name: Cordoba, the meeting with Ibn Rushd
stops.campa: Under pretext of business his father brings him, still beardless, into the house of Abu al-Walid Ibn Rushd, the great philosopher and qadi, who has asked to see the boy whose gifts are already spoken of. Ibn Rushd rises and embraces him and says only, 'Yes.' The boy answers, 'Yes,' then, seeing what had prompted the philosopher's pleasure, says, 'No' — and Ibn Rushd's color changes. Pressed directly whether mystical unveiling confirms what speculative reason arrives at, the youth answers: 'Yes and no. Between the yes and the no, spirits take their flight from their matter, and necks are separated from their bodies.'
stops.quote: Yes and no. Between the yes and the no, spirits take their flight from their matter, and necks are separated from their bodies.
stops.quote_source: Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, Ibn Arabi's own account of the meeting (trans. after Henry Corbin)
suggested_refs: The house of Ibn Rushd (Averroes) in Cordoba, where the two are said to have met
sources: Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya (trans. cited in sunofwest.com, 'Meeting with Ibn Rushd')
futmak.com, 'Ibn Arabi's meeting with Ibn Rushd in Cordoba'
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Seville, Abu al-Abbas al-Uryabi, the first master
stops.campa: In Seville he takes his first Sufi master: Abu al-Abbas al-Uryabi, an illiterate peasant of no worldly standing whose spiritual rank the young seeker recognizes at once beneath the plain surface. Ibn Arabi will walk, in the years that follow, the length and breadth of al-Andalus and the Maghrib in search of such men and women — the unlettered saints the learned overlook — sitting at their feet, testing his own openings against theirs, gathering the living chain of the Sufi masters he will later catalogue by name.
suggested_refs: Ibn Arabi's Ruh al-Quds and al-Durrat al-Fakhirah, his catalogues of the Andalusi and Maghribi masters
sources: Ibn Arabi, Ruh al-Quds (Sufis of Andalusia)
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Seville, the grave illness and the retreat under al-Urayni
stops.campa: A fever takes him so far down that the household gives him up for dead. Within, menacing figures press in to destroy him; then a being of great strength and sweetness rises among them, carrying a scent he can taste in his own breath, and scatters them by presence alone. He asks who it is. 'I am Surat Yasin,' it answers, 'I am your guard.' He surfaces to find his father at the bedside reciting that very sura. Risen, he gives up his family's plans entirely — no career, no property — and passes months in retreat under his first master, the illiterate al-Uryabi, refining the seizure of grace into a discipline.
stops.quote: I am Surat Yasin, I am your guard.
stops.quote_source: The figure seen in Ibn Arabi's death-fever, in his own account of the illness
suggested_refs: Ibn Arabi's account of his illness and the vision of Surat Yasin at his sickbed
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Stephen Hirtenstein, The Unlimited Mercifier

stops.name: Cordoba, the vision of all the prophets
stops.campa: In Cordoba he receives a vision that will not bear fruit in writing for another forty years: he sees all the prophets from Adam to Muhammad, each given, in the unseen, a particular Word by which the truth of existence is disclosed through him — Adam the Word of the divine form, Seth the Word of the gift, and so to Muhammad, in whom all the Words are gathered. He tells no one for decades. When at last he sets it down in Damascus it will be called Fusus al-Hikam, the Bezels of Wisdom, and become his most contested and most read book.
suggested_refs: Fusus al-Hikam (Bezels of Wisdom), whose seed vision is dated by tradition to this Cordoba year
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi, Fusus al-Hikam, prologue tradition

stops.name: Seville, Fatima bint al-Muthanna, the divine mother
stops.campa: He serves for nearly two years — longer than with any other master — a woman past ninety-five named Fatima bint al-Muthanna, a Cordoban living out her old age in Seville, who eats almost nothing yet keeps a fresh and rosy face, which he takes as a sign of a body wholly surrendered to God. She recites the Fatiha and it stands up before them in the air as a shape of light. She tells him plainly: 'I am your divine mother, and the light of your earthly mother.' With two companions he builds her a hut of reeds to live out her days in.
stops.quote: I am your divine mother, and the light of your earthly mother.
stops.quote_source: Ibn Arabi, Ruh al-Quds (Sufis of Andalusia)
suggested_refs: Ibn Arabi's Ruh al-Quds, chapter on Fatima bint al-Muthanna of Cordoba, whom he served at Seville
sources: Ibn Arabi, Ruh al-Quds
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Marchena, Shams, Mother of the Poor
stops.campa: At Marchena, south of Seville, he sits with another of the women masters he will not let history forget: Shams, called Umm al-Fuqara, Mother of the Poor, who feeds and shelters wandering Sufis from her own hand though she owns almost nothing. Among the unlettered peasants, the widows, and the old women of the Andalusi countryside he finds, again and again, a sanctity the jurists of the cities never think to look for; he will set their names down beside the famous men's in his book of masters so that they are not lost.
suggested_refs: Ibn Arabi's Ruh al-Quds, chapter on Shams, Mother of the Poor, of Marchena
sources: Ibn Arabi, Ruh al-Quds
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Tunis, al-Mahdawi and the Vast Earth
stops.campa: His first journey outside al-Andalus and the Maghrib proper takes him to Tunis, to Shaykh Abd al-Aziz al-Mahdawi, a master of great subtlety in the science of letters and numbers. Under his guidance Ibn Arabi enters the spiritual station he will call 'God's Vast Earth' — the earth of which the Qur'an says the servant may find room in it though the visible world seems to close on every side. Al-Mahdawi's copy of al-Tirmidhi's Khatm al-Awliya, on the Seal of the Saints, becomes for him a text he will spend a lifetime answering and completing.
suggested_refs: Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi's Khatm al-Awliya, which Ibn Arabi read with al-Mahdawi in Tunis
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the West (1165-1200)'

stops.name: Seville, Mashahid al-Asrar, the first book
stops.campa: Home from Tunis, he sets pen to paper for the first time as an author of visionary works: Mashahid al-Asrar, the Contemplation of the Holy Mysteries, opens a writing life that will run to several hundred titles before it ends in Damascus. What had been kept as private unveilings among the masters of Andalusia begins now to be written for others, in the elliptical, layered Arabic that will make him the most argued-over author in the later history of Islamic thought — too plain to some, too veiled to others, exactly calibrated to himself.
suggested_refs: Mashahid al-Asrar (Contemplation of the Holy Mysteries), his first written work
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, list of writings

stops.name: Fez, after the death of his parents
stops.campa: With both parents now dead, Ibn Arabi crosses into Morocco with his two sisters and settles for a time in Fez, city of the Idrisid founders and of the Qarawiyyin mosque-university, already for centuries a capital of Maghribi learning. Here he takes further masters, among them Muhammad ibn Qasim al-Tamimi, and continues the same labor as in Andalusia: seeking out the hidden poles and axes of the age, men the marketplace does not know are anything more than shopkeepers or day-laborers, and placing himself under their instruction without regard to rank.
suggested_refs: The Qarawiyyin Mosque of Fez, oldest continuously operating seat of learning in the Islamic world
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the West (1165-1200)'

stops.name: Fez, Badr al-Habashi becomes his companion
stops.campa: In Fez, in the year 594, a young man named Abdallah Badr al-Habashi attaches himself to Ibn Arabi and does not leave his side again for the rest of both their lives: through Egypt, Mecca, Anatolia, and Damascus, Badr will serve as companion, copyist, and the disciple to whom the master dictates commentaries at the request of others. It is one of the great friendships of the Sufi record, the kind the tradition calls suhba, companionship, in which years of shared road count for more than any single teaching.
suggested_refs: Abdallah Badr al-Habashi, lifelong companion first met in Fez in 594 AH
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, biographical notes on Badr al-Habashi

stops.name: Fez, the Night-Journey, Kitab al-Isra
stops.campa: In Fez comes a vision of ascension modeled on the Prophet's own Night-Journey: Ibn Arabi is raised in spirit through the heavens, station by station, receiving from each a knowledge proper to it, until he stands in the Presence beyond all station. He sets the whole account down as Kitab al-Isra ila Maqam al-Asra, the Book of the Night-Journey to the Station of the Nearest, one of his earliest sustained visionary compositions and the template for the vaster architecture of ascents he will build in the Futuhat in Mecca a few years on.
suggested_refs: Kitab al-Isra ila Maqam al-Asra (Book of the Night-Journey), composed in Fez
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, list of writings

segments.name: The Last Farewell to the West

stops.name: Cordoba, the funeral of Ibn Rushd
stops.campa: Averroes had been exiled and his books burned by decree of the Almohad caliph, then pardoned and recalled to Marrakesh, dying back in favor in December 1198; now, some three months on, his remains come home to Cordoba for burial. Ibn Arabi, now thirty-three, stands and watches the bier arrive laden on one flank of a pack-animal, the philosopher's own books tied to the other flank to counterweight the coffin. He says only: 'On one side the Master, on the other his books!' — and asks in verse whether the man's hopes were ever answered.
stops.quote: On one side the Master, on the other his books!
stops.quote_source: Ibn Arabi's remark at Ibn Rushd's funeral cortege, Cordoba, recorded in al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya
suggested_refs: The counterweighted bier of Averroes, books against corpse, entering Cordoba
sources: Explore Cordoba, 'Averroes of Cordoba'
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Murcia, farewell to al-Andalus
stops.campa: A vision in these months commands him to leave the West and go east: he does not resist it, only settles his remaining affairs. He returns once more to his birth-city of Murcia to take leave of it as of a person, the ground of the earliest visions, the parish of his father's service to the fallen emir. He knows, though nothing in the vision tells him so in words, that he will not walk this soil again; the tradition remembers this as his true farewell to Spain, though the geography of his going will carry him first south and only then east.
suggested_refs: Murcia, birthplace and site of Ibn Arabi's traditional farewell to al-Andalus
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the West (1165-1200)'

stops.name: Gibraltar, the last crossing
stops.campa: He crosses the strait at Gibraltar for the last time in the year 596, the land of al-Andalus dropping away behind the boat's wake. He is thirty-four, and has spent every one of his years thus far between Murcia, Seville, Cordoba, and their surrounding towns, save for the two brief crossings to Tunis and Fez. He does not know yet that Damascus at the far end of the Mediterranean world will claim the last seventeen years of his life, only that the vision has said east, and the crossing here is the door.
suggested_refs: The Strait of Gibraltar, final crossing out of al-Andalus
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Sale, farewell to the master Yusuf al-Kumi
stops.campa: In the coastal town of Sale he takes final leave of Yusuf al-Kumi, one of the last of the Maghribi masters under whom he trained, closing a circle of instruction that has run since the illiterate al-Uryabi of Seville fifteen years before. The school of masters, women and men, lettered and unlettered, that has formed him across al-Andalus and the Maghrib is now complete; what remains is to carry what he has received to Mecca, to the House itself, and see what further is asked of him there.
suggested_refs: Sale, Morocco, site of Ibn Arabi's farewell to his last Maghribi teacher
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
sunofwest.com, list of Ibn Arabi's teachers

stops.name: Tunis, the second stay and the road east
stops.campa: He returns once more to Tunis, this time not to settle but to gather himself for the road to Mecca; he takes final leave of al-Mahdawi's circle. Behind him now lies the whole architecture of Andalusi and Maghribi Sufism, its illiterate saints and its women masters, its philosophers and its jurists; ahead lies a pilgrimage he will not, in the event, ever complete by returning home from. Tunis is the hinge: the last of the West he will linger in before Egypt and the Hijaz.
suggested_refs: Tunis, the port of Ibn Arabi's final departure from the Maghrib toward Mecca
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in Mecca (1201-04)'

stops.name: Cairo, the first passage through Egypt
stops.campa: On the road to the Hijaz he passes for the first time through Egypt and its capital, already a byword for the learning and the litigiousness of its jurists, who will in years to come be among his fiercest readers and fiercest critics. He does not linger; Cairo in 1201 is a waystation, the Nile crossed, the pyramids and the citadel of Saladin's line glimpsed, before the caravan routes take him on toward the Red Sea coast and the roads that converge on Mecca for the season of pilgrimage.
suggested_refs: The Ayyubid citadel of Cairo, seat of Saladin's line, passed on the road to the Hijaz
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Denis Gril, 'Ibn Arabi in Egypt' (Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi Society)

stops.name: Mecca, arrival for the Hajj
stops.campa: He arrives at Mecca in the year 598 and performs the Hajj, circling the Kaaba that has stood since Abraham raised its walls with Ishmael. He will stay in the sacred precinct three years, longer than any pilgrim's ordinary season, for what awaits him here is not the fulfillment of a single obligation but the opening of a work: it is in Mecca, before the House itself, that the Meccan Revelations — the book that will carry his name to the ends of the Islamic world — is first given to him as a project he cannot refuse.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba at Mecca, circumambulated by Ibn Arabi across three years of residence
sources: Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in Mecca (1201-04)'
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Mecca, the vision of the Youth at the Kaaba
stops.campa: Circling the House by night he is met by a fata, a Youth, who is neither wholly of this world nor apart from it: he speaks not, yet is spoken through; he moves not, yet is the ground of every motion; a being made, Ibn Arabi will say, of light and secret meanings folded into a human shape. Seven such theophanies are granted him in the course of the circumambulation, and it is under their dictation, he says plainly, that the vast book he is now to write takes its first ordinance and its architecture.
suggested_refs: The vision of the fata (Youth) at the Kaaba, opening chapter of al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya
sources: Michel Chodkiewicz, 'The Paradox of the Kaaba' (Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi Society)
Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, opening chapters

stops.name: Mecca, the household of Sheikh Makin al-Din and Nizam
stops.campa: He is received into the house of a learned Persian of Isfahan, Makin al-Din Abu Shuja, imam at the station of Abraham, and reads the hadith of al-Tirmidhi with him; from his sister Fakhr al-Nisa, the old shaykha of the Hijaz, he takes a licence to transmit. And there is the daughter. Nizam, named Eye of the Sun and the Glory: riveting to look at, who adorns her father's assemblies, delights whoever is speaking and confounds her equals. If she declaims, he writes, Quss ibn Saida would fall silent. Accused later of a poet's ordinary infatuation, he answers that every name in the book means her, and means also what is beyond her.
stops.quote: She adorned the assemblies, delighting whoever was addressing the gathering and confounding her peers.
stops.quote_source: Preface to the Tarjuman al-Ashwaq (trans. Jane Clark after R. A. Nicholson)
suggested_refs: Tarjuman al-Ashwaq (The Interpreter of Desires), the sixty-one odes composed in Nizam's honor
sources: Ibn Arabi, Tarjuman al-Ashwaq, preface (trans. Jane Clark, Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi Society)
Michael Sells, 'Translator of Desires' (Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi Society)

stops.name: Mecca, the command to write al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya
stops.campa: The seven theophanies of the Kaaba and the years of residence in the sacred precinct crystallize into a single commission, understood by him as laid on him from beyond himself: to set down, chapter by chapter, everything unveiled to him of the divine sciences, the stations of the path, the secrets of the letters and the numbers and the Names — a book with no fixed limit, that he will still be adding to on his deathbed in Damascus forty years hence. He begins it here, in Mecca, and gives it the name it will keep: al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, the Meccan Revelations.
suggested_refs: Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, begun in Mecca, his single largest work
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in Mecca (1201-04)'

stops.name: Mecca, the meeting with Majduddin Ishaq
stops.campa: At Mecca he falls into friendship with Majduddin Ishaq ibn Yusuf, a native of Malatya in Anatolia and a man of high standing at the Seljuk court of Rum, who has come to make the Hajj. The vizier presses him to come north with him into the lands of the Seljuk sultan; Ibn Arabi, whose vision has never named an endpoint, only a direction, agrees. It is a friendship that will in time bind their two households into one, and carry the Andalusi master's teaching into the heart of Anatolia and, through it, toward a boy not yet born who will be called Jalal al-Din Rumi.
suggested_refs: Majduddin Ishaq ibn Yusuf al-Rumi, vizier of Malatya, whose friendship opens the Anatolian years
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, biographical notes on Majduddin Ishaq

segments.name: Baghdad, Mosul, Jerusalem: the Wandering Years

stops.name: Baghdad, twelve days in the City of Peace
stops.campa: He enters Baghdad, the old seat of the Abbasid caliphs, city of al-Junayd and al-Hallaj before him, and stays only twelve days: long enough to pay his respects to its scholars and its shrines, not long enough to be claimed by it, for his heart is set on Mosul, where an old friend of a nearer master waits. Baghdad in these years is diminished from its ancient splendor but still the nominal center of the Sunni world; he passes through it as a pilgrim passes through a capital, reverent and unhurried toward his true errand.
suggested_refs: Baghdad, seat of the Abbasid caliphate, visited for twelve days
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the East (1204-40)'

stops.name: Mosul, the khirqa of Khidr
stops.campa: In Mosul he keeps Ramadan and seeks out Ali ibn Abdallah ibn Jami, who lives in a garden outside the walls. Years before, on that ground, Khidr — the Green One, deathless guide of wayfarers since Moses met him at the meeting of the two seas — had with his own hands invested Ibn Jami with the mantle, the hidden saint Qadib al-Ban standing witness. Now Ibn Jami sets that same khirqa on Ibn Arabi, on the same spot, so that the chain reaching him passes through no lineage of the living but comes down from the deathless one directly. He composes here the Tanazzulat al-Mawsiliyya.
suggested_refs: The khirqa of Khidr, received by Ali ibn Jami from Khidr himself and passed by him to Ibn Arabi in the garden outside Mosul
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the East (1204-40)'

stops.name: Jerusalem, at the Farthest Mosque
stops.campa: He comes to Jerusalem, the al-Aqsa from which the Prophet made his own Night-Journey and ascension, the model his own Kitab al-Isra in Fez had followed. He prays in the precinct of the Dome and the Farthest Mosque, at the place the Qur'an calls the site blessed round about, and continues south and west again toward Egypt, in a year of restless movement between the holy cities of three empires — Ayyubid, Seljuk, Abbasid — none of which he stays long enough to call, in any worldly sense, his own.
suggested_refs: Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock, Jerusalem, visited on the road between Mosul and Cairo
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the East (1204-40)'

stops.name: Cairo, the second passage and the hostility of the jurists
stops.campa: He returns to Egypt in the year 603 and finds the climate for his teaching sharper than before: the exoteric jurists of Cairo, custodians of the letter of the law, hear reports of a man who speaks of the Seal of the Saints and of a love for God that outruns their categories, and murmur heresy. His companion Badr al-Habashi and the small circle of disciples gathered around him shield him from the worst of it; he does not moderate a syllable of what he teaches, only moves on again once the season allows, toward Mecca and the Hijaz he has never really left in spirit.
suggested_refs: The tension between Ibn Arabi's teaching and Cairo's exoteric jurists, recurring across his Egyptian visits
sources: Denis Gril, 'Ibn Arabi in Egypt' (Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi Society)
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Mecca, the return
stops.campa: He comes back once more to Mecca, closing a wide loop that has carried him from the Hijaz to Baghdad, Mosul, Jerusalem, and Cairo and now home again to the House. Each return to Mecca in these years functions for him as a kind of tuning: whatever has been gathered on the road — a khirqa in Mosul, a hostility survived in Cairo, a prayer completed in Jerusalem — is brought back and measured against the first commission received here, the writing of the Futuhat, which grows steadily under his hand no matter what city currently holds him.
suggested_refs: Mecca, the recurring axis to which Ibn Arabi's eastern travels return across a decade
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in Mecca (1201-04)'

stops.name: Konya, first arrival in the Seljuk capital
stops.campa: He comes north at last to Konya, capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, in the company of men bound to Majduddin Ishaq's household. The city that will one day be synonymous with Jalal al-Din Rumi and the whirling of the Mevlevi order is, in this year, simply the seat of a Turkish sultan friendly to Sufis and philosophers alike; Ibn Arabi is received at court, and the seed of a teaching lineage that will run through Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi to Rumi's own circle a generation later is quietly planted, though no one present can yet see the shape it will take.
suggested_refs: Konya, capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, later the city of Rumi and the Mevlevi order
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the East (1204-40)'

stops.name: Malatya, a household in Anatolia
stops.campa: He settles for long stretches at Malatya, in south-eastern Anatolia, Majduddin Ishaq's own city, and here for the first time in his life keeps something like a settled household: a wife, and in time at least two sons and a daughter. It is an unexpected late chapter for a man who has spent forty years as a wanderer among masters and shrines, and it grounds the last phase of his teaching in ordinary domestic time even as the Futuhat continues to grow, chapter on chapter, in whatever hours the household leaves him.
suggested_refs: Malatya, Ibn Arabi's Anatolian household and the raising of his children
sources: Ibn Arabi Society, 'Ibn 'Arabi in the East (1204-40)'
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Aleppo, the commentary on the Tarjuman al-Ashwaq
stops.campa: In Aleppo the jurists take offense at his love-poetry from the Meccan years, the odes for Nizam full of gazelles, wine, and the beloved's cheek, and charge that a Sufi shaykh has no business writing such things. His disciples Ibn Sawdakin and al-Habashi press him to answer; in the year 611 he sets down a line-by-line commentary, Dhakha'ir al-A'laq, showing that every gazelle and every cup names a station of the divine science and nothing of the flesh. It is read aloud in his lodging before the qadi's son Ibn al-Adim, who had doubted him — and who rises saying he will never again question a Sufi who claims a hidden sense in ordinary words.
suggested_refs: Dhakha'ir al-A'laq, Ibn Arabi's own commentary on the Tarjuman al-Ashwaq, written in Aleppo
sources: Ibn Arabi Society, notes on the composition of Dhakha'ir al-A'laq
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

stops.name: Malatya, the death of Majduddin and the guardianship of Qunawi
stops.campa: Majduddin Ishaq dies in the year 617, and Ibn Arabi, out of the old friendship struck in Mecca, marries his widow and takes into his own household the boy Sadr al-Din, barely a teenager. He raises and teaches him as his own, and the boy will grow to be the foremost systematizer of his stepfather's teaching, the man who gives Ibn Arabi's scattered unveilings the ordered philosophical shape by which later centuries, from Konya to Isfahan to Istanbul, will come to know the school of the Greatest Master.
suggested_refs: Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, stepson and foremost disciple, raised in Ibn Arabi's Malatya household
sources: Ibn Arabi Society, biographical notes on Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi
Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur

segments.name: Damascus: The Seal of the Saints

stops.name: Damascus, arrival and final settlement
stops.campa: After twenty-five years of wandering the Islamic world from Andalusia to Anatolia, at fifty-eight Ibn Arabi comes to Damascus, city of the Umayyad Mosque and the tomb of John the Baptist's head, then under the rule of the house of Saladin, and chooses it, without further vision or command needed, as the place he will not leave again. Patrons among the Ayyubid princes and the city's scholars gather round him; disciples begin to arrive from as far as Anatolia and Yemen; the seventeen years remaining to him will be the most settled and the most productive of his life.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque of Damascus, at the heart of the city Ibn Arabi chose as his final home
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Middle East Eye, 'Who was Ibn Arabi? The medieval Sufi master of Damascus'

stops.name: Damascus, the sea and the ocean: young Jalal al-Din Rumi
stops.campa: Through Damascus, fleeing the Mongol advance out of Balkh, passes the scholar Baha al-Din Walad with his household, his young son Jalal al-Din trailing behind him. Ibn Arabi, seeing the boy follow his father through the street, is said to have exclaimed: 'Praise be to God! An ocean walking behind a lake!' — reading in the child a depth the father, for all his learning, does not himself contain. The family continues on toward Konya, where in time the boy will become Mowlana, and where Ibn Arabi's own stepson Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi will number Rumi among his close companions.
stops.quote: Praise be to God! An ocean walking behind a lake!
stops.quote_source: Traditional Sufi hagiography of the Ibn Arabi-Rumi encounter; the meeting is not confirmed by contemporary sources and no early attribution has been traced
suggested_refs: Baha al-Din Walad's migration through Damascus with the young Jalal al-Din Rumi, en route to Konya
sources: Traditional Sufi hagiography (account widely repeated; early textual source not located)
Stephen Hirtenstein, cited discussions of the Ibn Arabi-Rumi encounter tradition

stops.name: Damascus, the Prophet's gift: Fusus al-Hikam
stops.campa: In the last ten days of Muharram, in the year 627, the Messenger of God appears to him in Damascus in a dream-vision of good news, holding a book in his hand. 'This is the book of the Fusus al-Hikam,' the Prophet tells him; 'take it and bring it out to men that they may benefit from it.' He wakes and sets down exactly what he has been given, without addition, he insists, of his own — the seed vision granted forty years before in Cordoba now delivered whole, chapter by chapter, prophet by prophet, into the book that will be argued over for the rest of Islamic history.
stops.quote: I saw the Messenger of God, may God bless him and give him peace, in a dream-vision of good news... in his hand was a book, and he said to me: this is the book of the Fusus al-Hikam; take it and bring it out to people who will benefit from it.
stops.quote_source: Ibn Arabi, Fusus al-Hikam, author's prologue
suggested_refs: Fusus al-Hikam (Bezels of Wisdom), delivered by dream-vision of the Prophet in Damascus, 627 AH
sources: Ibn Arabi, Fusus al-Hikam, prologue
ibnularabifoundation.org, Fusus al-Hikam critical edition

stops.name: Damascus, the first draft of al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya completed
stops.campa: Nearly thirty years after the commission was laid on him before the Kaaba, Ibn Arabi completes in December the first full draft of al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya: five hundred and sixty chapters gathering cosmology, law, the science of letters, the stations of the saints, and the whole architecture of a universe understood as the ceaseless self-disclosure of a single Reality wearing infinite forms. No book of comparable scope has come from a single hand in the Islamic tradition; he is not finished with it even now, and will spend the rest of his life expanding and correcting it.
suggested_refs: Al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, first complete draft, 560 chapters, finished in Damascus
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
William Chittick, The Sufi Path of Knowledge

stops.name: Damascus, the final recension of the Futuhat
stops.campa: Seven years on he completes a second, revised recension of the Futuhat, correcting, expanding, and reordering the vast text in his own hand, dictating to his students and copyists the final form by which it will be transmitted. He is seventy-three. The autograph manuscript of this recension will survive, copied and recopied across the Islamic world from Fez to Java, so that a reader in Damascus in 1238 and a reader in Istanbul four centuries later hold, chapter for chapter, the same book he considered finished only at the very end of his life.
suggested_refs: The 1238 autograph recension of al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya, the base text for all later manuscripts
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
William Chittick, The Sufi Path of Knowledge

stops.name: Damascus, the death of the Greatest Master
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of Rabi al-Thani in the year 638, at seventy-five, Ibn Arabi dies in Damascus, in the house of the qadi Muhyi al-Din ibn al-Zaki who had sheltered and honored him through his last years. Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, his stepson and the keeper of his teaching, is at hand; word runs out through the city and through the network of disciples that has grown up from Andalusia to Anatolia to Yemen that the Seal of the Muhammadan Saints, as he called the station he claimed for himself, has returned to the source of every station.
suggested_refs: The house of the qadi Muhyi al-Din ibn al-Zaki in Damascus, where Ibn Arabi died
sources: Claude Addas, Quest for the Red Sulphur
Encyclopedia.com, 'Ibn al-'Arabi (1165-1240)'

stops.name: Damascus, burial at the foot of Mount Qasiyun
stops.campa: He is carried up into the Salihiyya quarter, on the lower slope of Mount Qasiyun above the city, and buried in the family plot of the Banu Zaki, his patrons and protectors, among cypress and the graves of the district's scholars. For nearly three centuries the grave draws only local visitors and a few devoted Sufis; the wider Islamic world has not yet decided what to make of him, and in some quarters his name is still spoken with suspicion. The mountain keeps him quietly, waiting for the century that will make his resting place a place of state.
suggested_refs: The Banu Zaki family cemetery on Mount Qasiyun, Salihiyya, Ibn Arabi's original burial ground
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ibn Arabi'
Damas Cultural Society, 'Damascus, Salihiyya: Sh. Muhyiddin Ibn al-Arabi'

stops.name: Damascus, Sultan Selim I raises the mosque over the tomb
stops.campa: The master had left a riddle in letters behind him: when the Sin enters the Shin, the tomb of Muhyi al-Din will appear. Two hundred and seventy-six years pass, the grave under rubbish and rubble, and then Selim — Salim, the Sin — enters al-Sham, the Shin, and the sentence closes like a lock. He takes Damascus in 922, guided, the tradition says, by a dream to the neglected ground on Qasiyun. Returning from Egypt he raises over it a mosque, a tekke, a mausoleum: the first Ottoman building in Syria. Three centuries on the exiled emir Abd al-Qadir al-Jaza'iri chooses this ground, and lies down beside the master whose books had made him.
stops.quote: When the Sin enters the Shin, there will appear the tomb of Muhyi al-Din.
stops.quote_source: Prophecy attributed to Ibn Arabi, read as foretelling Selim I's entry into al-Sham; traditional, cf. the Shajara al-Nu'maniyya literature
suggested_refs: The Salimiyya Takiyya, Damascus, built 924 AH / 1518-19 by Sultan Selim I over Ibn Arabi's tomb
The tomb of Abd al-Qadir al-Jaza'iri, interred in the same Salihiyya precinct in 1883 (see abdelkader.journey.json)
sources: Archnet, 'Shrine of Ibn al-'Arabi, Damascus, Syria'
Denis Gril, 'The Enigma of the Shajara al-Nu'maniyya' (Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi Society), on the Sin/Shin prophecy
Wikipedia, 'Salimiyya Takiyya'
Itzchak Weismann, 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jazairi: God and the Perfect Man' (Muhyiddin Ibn Arabi Society)
